facts.text: Gebisa Ejeta was born in Wollonkomi, Ethiopia, to Oromo parents.
facts.quote: Ejeta was born in the remote village Wollonkomi, Ethiopia to Oromo parents.

facts.text: Encouraged by his mother, Ejeta walked 20 kilometres to the nearest elementary school every Sunday evening to stay there for the week.
facts.quote: Encouraged by his mother, he walked 20 kilometres to the nearest elementary school every Sunday evening and spend the week there.

facts.text: During primary school, Ejeta intended to study engineering when he reached college age.
facts.quote: During primary school, Ejeta planned to study engineering when he reached college age.

facts.text: Ejeta's mother convinced him that he could accomplish more by working in agriculture.
facts.quote: However, his mother convinced him he could do more working in agriculture.

facts.text: With help from Oklahoma State University, Ejeta attended an agricultural and technical secondary school in Ethiopia and studied at what is now Haramaya University.
facts.quote: With assistance from the Oklahoma State University, he attended an agricultural and technical secondary school in Ethiopia, and also studied at what is now Haramaya University.

facts.text: Ejeta earned his master's and doctoral degrees in plant breeding and genetics from Purdue University in 1976 and 1978, respectively.
facts.quote: Ejeta received his master's and doctoral degrees in plant breeding and genetics from Purdue in 1976 and 1978, respectively.

facts.text: After receiving his doctorate from Purdue in 1978, Ejeta went to work in rain-starved northern Sudan.
facts.quote: His work took him to rain-starved northern Sudan after receiving a doctoral degree in plant breeding and genetics from Purdue in 1978.

facts.text: In the early 1980s, after five years of research in northern Sudan, Ejeta developed Hageen Dura-1, Africa's first commercial drought-tolerant sorghum hybrid.
facts.quote: Five years of research in rain-starved northern Sudan produced his first breakthrough in sorghum research in the early 1980s, when Ejeta developed the drought-tolerant cultivar Hageen Dura-1, the first commercial sorghum hybrid in Africa.

facts.text: Hageen Dura-1 produced yields up to 150 percent higher than traditional sorghum cultivars.
facts.quote: Hageen Dura-1 produced yields up to 150 percent higher than traditional sorghum cultivars.

facts.text: About 1 million acres of Hageen Dura-1 sorghum are grown in Sudan each year.
facts.quote: About 1 million acres of the drought-tolerant sorghum is grown in Sudan annually.

facts.text: Ejeta joined the faculty at Purdue University in 1984.
facts.quote: He joined the Purdue faculty in 1984.

facts.text: Working with Purdue colleague Larry Butler, Ejeta identified the chemical exudate from sorghum that attracts parasitic Striga rootlets.
facts.quote: Working with late Purdue colleague Larry Butler, Ejeta identified the exudate - chemical signal - from sorghum that is picked up by Striga rootlets.

facts.text: Ejeta developed a biological mechanism to disrupt the chemical signal that attracts Striga to sorghum.
facts.quote: From there, he was able to develop a biological mechanism for interrupting the exudation process.

facts.text: In 1994, eight tons of Ejeta's drought-tolerant and Striga-resistant sorghum seeds grown at a Purdue research farm were distributed to twelve African nations.
facts.quote: In 1994 eight tons of Ejeta's drought-tolerant and Striga-resistant sorghum seeds produced at a Purdue agricultural research farm were distributed to Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Mozambique, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia, Sudan, Tanzania and Zimbabwe.

facts.text: Farmers who planted the distributed seeds reported sorghum yields up to four times larger than traditional crops.
facts.quote: Farmers reported yields of as much as four times larger than traditional sorghum crops.

facts.text: Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and World Food Prize Foundation President Kenneth Quinn announced Ejeta's World Food Prize at the U.S. Department of State.
facts.quote: The award announcement was made at the U.S. Department of State in Washington, D.C., by Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and World Food Prize Foundation President Kenneth Quinn.

facts.text: Ejeta received the World Food Prize on October 15, 2009, for developing sorghum varieties resistant to drought and Striga.
facts.quote: On Thursday (Oct. 15), the plant breeder and geneticist received the World Food Prize for his work in developing sorghum varieties resistant to drought and Striga, a parasitic weed common on the African continent.

facts.text: President Barack Obama appointed Ejeta to the Board for International Food and Agricultural Development in 2011.
facts.quote: In 2011 President Barack Obama appointed Gebisa Ejeta as Member, Board for International Food and Agricultural Development.

facts.text: President Biden awarded Ejeta the National Medal of Science in 2023.
facts.quote: The National Medal of Science was awarded to Ejeta by President Biden in 2023.
